analysis.one_liner: Tightens disclosure rules to curb overcharging by Pentagon defense contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: after being referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee in June 2023, it sat untouched until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require defense contractors bidding on no-bid (sole-source) and cost-reimbursement contracts to give the Pentagon their actual cost and pricing data. It would narrow a loophole that lets contractors label their products 'commercial items' and avoid justifying their prices, cap the advance payments the Pentagon gives traditional contractors unless they hand over cost information on time, and require major defense contractors to file annual public reports on their profit margins and pricing decisions. The goal is to stop companies from raising prices to the Pentagon faster than their own costs rise — costs that are paid by taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund roughly $800 billion a year in defense spending, would gain if the bill made contractor pricing more honest. Regular troops and the Pentagon's own budget office also benefit when the department pays less for the same equipment. Military families ultimately pay as taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires cost or pricing data from contractors on sole-source and cost-reimbursement contracts, so the Pentagon can see what a product actually costs before paying a price.

Narrows the 'commercial item' definition so contractors cannot dodge price justification by calling products commercial unless they had real price competition with at least two viable offers and actual prior sales in like quantities.

Creates a pilot limiting progress payments to traditional contractors at 50%, rising only to 80% or 95% if the company submits certified cost data within 30 days of a Pentagon request — tying advance cash to cooperation on pricing.

Requires traditional defense contractors to report annually on sales volumes, prices, gross margins, cost changes, and a detailed narrative of their pricing strategy — including why prices rose faster than costs — and requires the Pentagon to publish these reports on a public website.

analysis.who_pays: Large traditional defense contractors would bear new reporting costs and could face lower prices and reduced advance cash flow on sole-source work. Some commercial suppliers might avoid selling to the Pentagon rather than open their books, which could shrink the supplier pool.

drawbacks.text: Tightening the 'commercial item' definition and requiring certified cost data raises compliance costs and could discourage commercial firms — including newer, non-traditional suppliers — from bidding on Pentagon work, reducing the competition the Pentagon wants.
Capping progress payments at 50% could strain the cash flow of contractors that finance production up front, potentially raising costs or delaying deliveries even for companies acting in good faith.

The bill adds reporting and negotiation overhead for both contractors and Pentagon acquisition staff without changing the underlying budgets, so some of the savings could be absorbed by administrative cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — forcing companies with no competition to justify their prices to the customer paying them — is real and aims at a documented pattern of contractor margins rising faster than costs. The costs are administrative and cash-flow burdens that mostly hit the same large contractors the bill targets, plus some risk of driving commercial suppliers away. On balance the design is a modest, targeted transparency measure rather than a sweeping overhaul; its practical impact depends entirely on whether the Pentagon actually uses the data to push prices down.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on June 20, 2023, joined by a Republican cosponsor, Sen. Mike Braun.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee on the day of introduction.
The only subsequent action was a star print ordered on July 19, 2023; the committee never held a markup, and the bill never reached the floor.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill receiving a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large defense contractors are better off: they keep charging sole-source prices without public margin disclosure, price-justification requirements, or payment caps. The Pentagon acquisition process stays as it is, and no taxpayer savings materialize.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense contractors keeping current pricing practices

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Pentagon Price Gouging Act in the Senate.

against.name: Sen. Jack Reed
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup; it received no action after the July 2023 star print.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democrat as sponsor and one of the 49 Senate Republicans as cosponsor — but it never got a vote, so no vote-based partisan split exists.

industries.industry: Large traditional defense contractors (sole-source weapons and services suppliers)
industries.note: The bill would require them to disclose margins and pricing strategy publicly, justify sole-source prices with cost data, and accept capped advance payments. Their profits on sole-source and cost-reimbursement work depend on prices set without rigorous cost scrutiny, which runs against the taxpayer's interest in honest prices.

industries.industry: Commercial suppliers and non-traditional vendors selling to the Pentagon
industries.note: Narrowing the 'commercial item' definition removes an exemption that made selling to the Pentagon easier, which could deter some commercial firms — though suppliers facing genuine two-way price competition would remain exempt from cost-data requirements.
